title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop affects verifier-detected safety violations for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier and subjected to up to one automated repair iteration if the verifier flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test (executor's exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention) produced p = 1.00. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks: translating operator intent to device configuration, multi-step change planning, and programmatic repairs. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms—which motivate verifier-in-the-loop architectures [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A common operational pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): generate a candidate, verify formally, and repair or escalate violations.

Controlled measurements isolating the marginal contribution of deterministic verifiers (holding the model’s proposal fixed) are scarce. Operators need to know: when an LLM already produces high-quality proposals, how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated repair budget provide on an operational pass/fail metric? We address this specific operational question by preregistering and executing a paired experiment that holds the LLM proposal identical across arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics) and measures verifier-scoped pass/fail outcomes under a concrete model+validator pairing.
sections.related_work:
Formal, deterministic network-verification methods (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers, Batfish-style analyzers) provide machine-checkable properties such as reachability, isolation, and update atomicity and form the technical backbone of verifier-in-the-loop designs in NetOps [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems integrate LLMs for intent parsing and configuration generation while explicitly recommending guardrails for reliability (e.g., INTA, Confucius, and other agentic NetOps frameworks) [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Across structured-generation domains, generate–verify–repair or critic-in-the-loop patterns are proposed to reduce unsafe outputs [PoeTone; INTA].

Complementary literature documents LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors—and recommends verifiers or human oversight as mitigations [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. However, the supplied record set lacks a controlled, preregistered ablation that quantifies a verifier's marginal effect while keeping the LLM's initial output identical for both arms; our work provides such an artifact-backed measurement and situates it relative to these system-level recommendations.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026 and froze the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, task seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule prior to observing outcomes. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will have a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations. The preregistration and supporting artifacts are archived and recorded in the execution manifest (preregistration SHA-256 present in the manifest).

Task corpus and stratification. We generated a deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds and deterministic replacement rules. Tasks were stratified into three clusters per the preregistration: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), and static-route-change (166); these realized per-cluster counts match the preregistered allocation and are confirmed in the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl (manifest archived in the evidence bundle). The task generator constrained allowed_features to {admin, mtu, vlan} to match the verifier’s coverage.

Generation semantics and isolation. To isolate verifier+repair impact we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false). For each task the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal; that identical candidate served as both the baseline output and the starting point for the guarded arm. The guarded arm invoked the automated single-repair call only if the deterministic verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on the shared candidate. This design intentionally prevents verifier-guided regeneration and measures the marginal effect of verification plus at most one repair applied to the same initial proposal.

Model, adapter, and verifier. The requested model was gpt-5-mini called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); model configuration (max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation) is archived in execution/model_configuration.json. The deterministic verifier used for gating and scoring was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the validator specification and the mapping of violation codes to severity are included in the archived validator-spec artifacts. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistration.

Analysis plan and exact test. The preregistered confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implements the exact two-sided McNemar by forming n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs) and performing an exact binomial test on the observed n10 count under X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5); the two-sided p-value is computed as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} truncated at 1.0. We also computed paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference using B = 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), sampling pairs with replacement while preserving pairing. Missingness, retries, and stopping rules followed the preregistered contract and are described and archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcome. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv) and the deterministic_reconciliation manifest confirm these counts.

Exact test and CI. Under the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention the two-sided p-value for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1) is p = 1.00. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Both computations are recorded in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl in the evidence bundle.

Discordant episode: deterministic identifier and artifact-backed summary. The single discordant episode (the one pair where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) is recorded in the archived execution/raw_results.jsonl with deterministic identifier pair-000389. The archived validator_trace for pair-000389 reports a single medium-severity violation classified as an ACL-scope policy/intent mismatch (violation code ACL-MISCONFIG-MED per the archived validator-spec); the guarded repair-stage call generated a targeted repair that added a missing ACL entry to satisfy the preregistered intent constraints. After the repair the verifier reported zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations and the task was recorded as a guarded success. All per-task provider-call traces, repair prompts/responses, and the validator_trace for pair-000389 are archived under execution/* and can be inspected deterministically via the execution/raw_results.jsonl entry for pair-000389. (The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json confirm exactly one repair-stage call was observed and that it produced the single discordant conversion.)

Secondary diagnostics and power. The preregistration assumed a baseline error prevalence p_b ≈ 0.30 for power planning; the observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) was far lower, producing a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements. Consequently, secondary per-violation-class analyses were uninformative due to near-zero counts; the related CSV diagnostics (analysis/missingness_summary.csv, analysis/contamination_summary.csv) record zero exclusions and zero failed episodes.

Representative exemplars. Representative per-task records (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json etc.) illustrate typical configurations and verifier diagnostics where both arms passed. The archived exemplar for pair-000389 includes the initial shared candidate, the verifier's reported violation codes/severity before repair, the repair prompt and response, and the final verifier_trace showing pass. These artifacts are all present in the evidence bundle and are sufficient for deterministic audit of the corrective event.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications. Under the constrained experimental regime—requested LLM gpt-5-mini, shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a narrow feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan, ACLs as modeled}), and at most one automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This conditional result documents a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high on verifier-modeled properties, the measurable marginal pass-rate gains from a modest verifier+repair budget may be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric. Nevertheless, the verifier produced concrete operational value by converting a single baseline failure (pair-000389) into a pass via a single automated repair.

Design-choice trade-offs. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolates the verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals—this suits deployment scenarios where the original proposal must be preserved for human review or when model-call budgets are constrained. Alternative operational choices—verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, retrieval- or history-augmented generation—may increase final-pass probability but at higher model-call cost and are outside this study's scope; each requires its own preregistration and measurement.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic task seeds, and deterministic replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity is limited by the verifier’s modeled property set: pass==no preregistered high/medium violations is defined relative to validator coverage and severity mapping archived in the validator-spec. If operators require properties outside that scope (vendor-specific behaviors, dynamic protocol states), measured pass-rate differences here underestimate the operational effect of broader verifier coverage. External validity is limited by single-model testing (requested gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and constrained feature scope; we do not claim cross-model or production generality.

Statistical nuance. The archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor’s exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs computation and the empirical discordant counts (n = 1). Small-sample exact p-values under this convention can be non-intuitive; p = 1.00 indicates the observed discordant pattern is not unusual under the null given n is small. The paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] complements this inference and quantifies sampling uncertainty for the absolute difference.

Practical recommendations. (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before investing in expensive repair budgets: when baseline error is extremely low on verifier-scoped properties, marginal pass-rate gains per unit cost may be small. (2) Align verifier property coverage with operator-critical constraints and extend verifier modeling where necessary. (3) Choose generation semantics to match deployment priorities: shared-initial semantics minimize model-call overhead and preserve the original proposal, while verifier-guided regeneration can increase final-pass probability at the cost of additional model calls.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), giving an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the run’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement illustrates a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high for verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, measurable marginal pass-rate benefit from a modest verifier+repair budget can be negligible on a composite pass/fail metric, though the verifier can still correct rare concrete failures (e.g., pair-000389). Practitioners should measure baseline error prevalence, align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties, and select generation/repair semantics that match deployment priorities. The full preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of every claim made here.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (pair-000389) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for the entry with pair_id == 'pair-000389' and inspect the archived validator_trace and repair_provider_trace for the pre-repair violation code, repair prompt/response, and post-repair verification outcome.
